No, it is not more correct to use Method 1 than Method 2.

In this hypothetical world, having a sister has a direct effect on blood pressure and heart condition. Blood pressure also has a direct effect on heart condition. This creates a confounding variable (blood pressure) that affects both the exposure (having a sister) and the outcome (heart condition). 

Method 1, which conditions on blood pressure, is essentially a form of stratification or matching. However, this method is still susceptible to confounding bias because it does not account for the direct effect of having a sister on blood pressure. In other words, even within the same blood pressure stratum, having a sister may still have an independent effect on heart condition.

Method 2, on the other hand, estimates the overall effect of having a sister on heart condition without conditioning on blood pressure. This approach is more likely to capture the total effect of having a sister on heart condition, including both the direct effect and the indirect effect through blood pressure.

In this scenario, using Method 2 is more correct because it provides a more comprehensive understanding of the causal relationship between having a sister and heart
